To inform this Series paper we reviewed epidemiological studies published over the past decade to describe the burden of key health outcomes among sex workers and associated factors contributing to these disparities. Within the mental health literature, we estimate at least one in four and as many as four in five sex workers experience depression. Within sexual and reproductive health literature, at least one in three sex workers are estimated to experience an unmet need for contraception. Using a Health Equity framework, we contextualise evidence gaps related to these health areas across multiple levels of influence (eg, systems of power, relationships and networks, physiological pathways, and individual factors) and offer recommendations to advance an agenda of health equity for sex workers in future research and programmes. Priority programme and policies include upholding the autonomy and dignity of sex worker communities, ensuring the inclusion of gender diverse populations in research, addressing structural determinants of health, and fostering meaningful community engagement and collaboration.

title: Towards occupational health and safety in sex work
abstract: Sex workers remain overwhelmingly excluded from occupational health and safety (OHS) protections due to continued criminalisation and stigmatisation of sex work. In this Series paper, we examine evidence on sex workers' OHS using an adapted OHS framework. Our findings show how criminalisation undermines comprehensive OHS practices across legislative contexts, but despite criminalisation, sex workers adopt innovative, community-driven strategies to safeguard OHS and place a strong emphasis on community mobilisation and mutual aid. Decriminalisation markedly improves working conditions and facilitates the development of sex worker-led official OHS guidelines. In contrast, legalisation can perpetuate many of the OHS barriers associated with criminalisation. OHS presents novel opportunities to create safer workplaces and advance the health and human rights of sex workers. Implementing OHS practices designed and led by sex workers with local expertise in their specific work environments is a crucial next step in advancing the health, safety, and labour rights of sex workers globally.

title: Violence prevention and support interventions for sex workers
abstract: Violence against sex workers can be substantial, with severe physical and mental health consequences. In this Series paper, we review the global evidence on violence prevention and support interventions by and for sex workers, and focus on violence reduction, mental health, and access to services. We found that peer-reviewed evidence focused on client-perpetrated violence, whereas non-peer-reviewed evidence focused on broader human rights abuses and police violence. The central involvement of sex workers in intervention design and delivery resulted in improved engagement and effectiveness in terms of reducing violence. Interventions that reduced violence from clients did not affect intimate partner violence, and vice versa. Peer networks strengthen agency through collective safety planning, information sharing, and emotional support, yet access is limited for migrant and street-based sex workers. Broader stakeholder engagement-including from police, policy makers, health and social services, and third parties such as managers and security-is essential for addressing structural determinants of violence, although reliance upon these same stakeholders can reinforce systems that perpetuate violence. Addressing violence requires interventions that recognise the diverse forms and perpetrators of violence, alongside broad structural reforms to tackle its root causes.

title: Accelerating action on road safety
abstract: Road traffic injuries remain a leading cause of death and disability globally. According to the latest analysis of the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023, published on July 20, 50·9 million people sustained road traffic injuries, and 1·34 million died in 2023. Children and young adults are disproportionately affected. Road injuries were the leading cause of death in males aged 10–39 years. Other striking inequities also exist. In low-income countries, people are six times more likely to die from road injuries than those in higher income countries despite a higher incidence of road injuries in high-income countries.

authors: The Editors of The Lancet Public Health

title: Impact of the Ultra Low Emission Zone on lung function growth in children in London, UK: a prospective parallel cohort study
abstract: Background Traffic-related air pollution is a risk factor for lung disease and early mortality. Clean air zones are public health policy interventions used to reduce traffic-related air pollution in urban areas, but evidence of their health benefits is limited. We describe a natural experiment study evaluating the impact of the Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) in London, UK. The primary aim was to assess the impact of the ULEZ on children's lung function growth trajectories, by comparing forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1 ) measurements over 5 years between children in London and Luton, UK. Methods The Children's Health in London and Luton (CHILL) study is a prospective, two-arm, parallel cohort study. We recruited children aged 6–9 years from primary schools in central London (the original area of the ULEZ implementation) and Luton (a comparator site with no clean air zone). Children were excluded if they had symptoms of lung disease (excluding asthma) or learning or physical disabilities preventing them from giving informed assent. Lung function was measured by spirometry at annual school visits at baseline (before ULEZ implementation) and over the following 4 years. Annual residential exposures to nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) and particulate matter with aerodynamic diameters of less than 10 μm (PM 10 ) and less than 2·5 μm (PM 2·5 ) were estimated at each child's home address at 20 m 2 resolution using a validated dispersion modelling system. The primary outcome was the annual rate of lung function growth, measured as post-bronchodilator FEV 1 over the 5-year study period. We assessed growth trajectories against individualised residential exposure to NO 2 , PM 10 , and PM 2·5 . We used mixed-effects linear regression to compare lung function growth between London and Luton and to examine associations between air pollution exposures and lung growth. Findings Of 122 schools approached, 84 (69%) agreed to participate (44 schools in London; 40 schools in Luton). Of 9419 children invited, we recruited 3414 children (1664 in London and 1750 in Luton) between June 5, 2018, and April 4, 2019, before ULEZ implementation. 3209 (94·0%) of 3414 children were included in the FEV 1 analysis (1557 children in London, 1652 children in Luton). Children were similar across the two sites in terms of age, height, and weight, with a higher proportion of girls in London (867 [56%] of 1557) than in Luton (809 [49%] of 1652). Baseline adjusted FEV 1 was lower in London than Luton (difference –38 mL, 95% CI –58 to –18; p=0·0002). At baseline, children's modelled annual exposures to NO 2 , the pollutant most reflective of exhaust emissions, were 18·95 μg/m 3 (95% CI 18·51 to 19·38; p<0·0001) higher in London than in Luton. Over the follow-up period, children's FEV 1 growth increased by 10 mL/year (95% CI 5 to 15; p=0·0002) more in London than in Luton (233 mL/year vs 223 mL/year), with modelled residential exposures to NO 2 decreasing faster in London than in Luton (decreases of –3·77 μg/m 3 per year in London vs –1·77 μg/m 3 per year in Luton; p<0·0001). After 4 years, mean FEV 1 reached parity across sites: 2283 mL (2207 to 2354) in London; 2282 mL (2185 to 2376) in Luton. The proportion of children with clinically impaired lung function fell from 184 (14%) of 1280 children to 51 (9%) of 585 children in London, and from 126 (9%) of 1339 children to 41 (7%) of 606 children in Luton. Interpretation Introduction of the London ULEZ was associated with improved lung function growth trajectories in children in London compared with children in Luton, suggesting that previous deficits in lung development were restored. This evidence supports wider implementation of clean air zones as a public health intervention. Funding National Institute for Health and Care Research and Natural Environment Research Council UK Research and Innovation.

title: Domain-specific physical activity levels and risk of dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Associations between physical activity and distinct health outcomes vary by domain (eg, leisure-time, occupational, household, or commuting); however, comparable evidence on dementia risk remains scarce. We aimed to examine the associations between domain-specific physical activity and risk of all-cause dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and vascular dementia. Methods In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we systematically searched PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science for cohort and case–control studies published between Jan 1, 2021, and May 2, 2026. We also included studies from a previous systematic review (from database inception to Oct 21, 2021) with the same search strategy and eligibility criteria. Eligible studies included adults aged 20 years or older with cognitive function assessed at baseline, physical activity measures, and at least 1 year of follow-up. Studies were appraised with the Rayyan web-based platform and summary data (relative risk [RR] and 95% CI) were extracted by up to six independent reviewers. Outcomes were all-cause dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and vascular dementia, analysed by multilevel random-effects meta-analyses. Study quality was assessed with an adapted scale. This study is registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251010899). Findings Among 6270 identified records, 17 studies were eligible for inclusion. Combined with 57 studies in the previous systematic review, we included 74 studies totalling 4 227 297 participants (2 230 046 [52·8%] female and 1 997 251 [47·2%] male; median age 67·3 years [IQR 56·5–74·1]). 40 (54%) studies were of moderate or high quality and 69 (93%) were conducted in high-income countries. Over a median follow-up of 10·0 years (IQR 5·1–21·3), high physical activity levels were associated with reduced risks of all-cause dementia (n=146 effect sizes; RR 0·80 [95% CI 0·75–0·86]; I 2 =97·4%), Alzheimer's disease (n=59; 0·79 [0·70–0·90]; I 2 =91·3%), and vascular dementia (n=21; 0·71 [0·58–0·87]; I 2 =77·5%); however, associations varied by domain. Leisure-time ( k =20 studies; n=33 effect sizes; RR 0·76 [95% CI 0·65–0·88]; I 2 =96·6%) and household ( k =1; 0·85 [0·74–0·98]) physical activity were associated with a reduced risk of all-cause dementia. By contrast, occupational ( k =5; 1·20 [1·01–1·42]; I 2 =85·6%) and commuting ( k =2; 1·10 [1·03–1·18]; I 2 =0·0%) physical activity were associated with an increased risk. Dose–response meta-analyses showed non-linear inverse associations for leisure-time and occupational activity. Certainty of evidence ranged from very low to low across domains. Interpretation The association between physical activity and dementia risk might be domain-specific. Public health strategies for the prevention of dementia should address equitable access to safe spaces for exercise, adequate leisure time, and mitigation strategies in occupational settings. Funding US National Institutes of Health, Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado do Rio Grande do Sul; the Brazilian National Council for Scientific and Technological Development; and Department of Science and Technology of Secretariat of Science, Technology, Innovation and Health Complex of Ministry of Health of Brazil.

title: Global and regional progress towards reduced burden of oral conditions between 2019 and 2023: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
authors: Sayed Muhammad Ata Ullah Shah Bukhari
Mauro Henrique Nogueira Guimarães De Abreu
abstract: BACKGROUND: WHO's Global Oral Health Action Plan (GOHAP) targets include a 10% relative reduction in the combined prevalence of main oral conditions by 2030. The first GOHAP evaluation was planned for 2023, with subsequent evaluations scheduled for 2026 and 2030. The aim of this systematic analysis of the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023 was to evaluate global and regional progress (2019-23) towards this target and related complementary indicators. METHODS: Using modelled estimates from epidemiological surveys and registries in 204 countries and territories, we estimated the age-standardised prevalence of untreated caries in deciduous and permanent teeth, severe periodontitis, edentulism, other oral disorders and orofacial clefts, and the age-standardised incidence of lip and oral cavity cancer. Progress towards GOHAP targets was measured by comparing the percentage change from 2019 to 2023 in the above indicators against the stated GOHAP target of a 10% relative reduction. FINDINGS: Globally, the age-standardised prevalence of main oral conditions declined (-1·55% [95% uncertainty interval -2·32 to -0·82]) between 2019 and 2023, but global cases increased by 3·07% (2·32 to 3·75), from 3·62 billion (3·35 to 3·95) to 3·73 billion (3·45 to 4·06). Among complementary indicators, reductions in age-standardised prevalence were observed for untreated caries in permanent teeth (-1·99% [-2·49 to -1·40]) whereas the age-standardised incidence of lip and oral cavity cancer increased (8·35% [0·13 to 16·32]), as did the age-standardised prevalence of orofacial clefts (2·25% [0·77 to 3·83]). Progress was heterogeneous across GBD super-regions, with south Asia having the largest reductions in the age-standardised prevalence of main oral conditions (-3·34% [-4·95 to -1·80]) and untreated caries in deciduous teeth (-9·09% [-17·62 to -0·08]). Sub-Saharan Africa showed the largest increase in prevalent cases of main oral conditions (9·51% [8·09-10·94]) and age-standardised incidence of lip and oral cavity cancer (14·86% [1·19-32·45]). The high-income super-region had an increase in the age-standardised prevalence of main oral conditions (1·24% [0·56-1·96]) and untreated caries in deciduous teeth (9·21% [6·60-11·89]). INTERPRETATION: Our modelled estimates of global trends in the prevalence of oral conditions from 2019 to 2023 suggest that early progress is modest and, at the current pace, insufficient to meet the 2030 GOHAP targets. Accelerated, equity-focused prevention and integration of essential oral health-care services within primary care and universal health coverage are needed, alongside strengthened oral cancer control and congenital anomaly care. FUNDING: The Gates Foundation.

title: The burden of low physical activity in Australia: a comprehensive comparative risk assessment
abstract: BACKGROUND: Estimating the effects of physical activity on disease burden is important to inform public health policies. Standard comparative risk assessments underestimate disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) attributable to low physical activity (LPA), because: (1) direct effects of physical activity on mental health and falls are not included, (2) impacts from changes in blood pressure, plasma glucose, LDL cholesterol, and bone mineral density are excluded, and (3) meta-analyses for relative risks (RRs) overadjust mediators. This study aimed to re-estimate DALYs attributable to LPA (activity below the >4200 metabolic minimum task mins per week minimum risk level) in Australia. METHODS: In this comparative risk assessment, we used the Australian Burden of Disease Study 2024 as the framework to assess DALYs attributable to LPA in Australia in calendar year 2024. Participants were Australians older than 20 years. In our analysis we also included associations of physical activity with depression and anxiety (and falls in sensitivity analyses), and the additional risk factors (high plasma glucose and diabetes, blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, and bone mineral density), from published systematic reviews and meta-analyses (and a bespoke analysis for LDL cholesterol). To account for the overadjustment of mediators, we calculated the RR overadjustment. FINDINGS: The DALYs attributable to LPA were 200 000 (95% uncertainty interval 146 000-254 000), which was 68·1% greater than the attributable burden using standard burden of disease study methods (119 000 DALYs [98 900-139 000]). Of this 81 000 DALYs (47 100-115 000) increase, 40 100 DALYs (29 300-50 900) were due to the direct effects on depression and anxiety, 24 900 DALYs (14 200-35 600) were due to including the additional disease effects from risk factors impacted by physical activity, and 15 900 DALYs (3180-28 700) were due to estimated mediator overadjustment. INTERPRETATION: Attributable burden of LPA in Australia is underestimated. This underestimation most probably also applies to LPA burden in other countries using standard methodologies. Expanding the model structure to comprehensively estimate the burden of LPA provides a more accurate assessment to inform public health interventions and prevention programmes. FUNDING: Australian Sports Commission.

title: Measuring the composition and availability of human resources for health by sex in 204 countries and territories, 1990–2023, and workforce gaps for universal health coverage: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
authors: Che Mohd Nasril Che Mohd Nassir
Mauro Henrique Nogueira Guimarães de Abreu
abstract: BACKGROUND: Understanding the size, gender composition, and cadre mix of the health workforce and how it has evolved across time and locations can inform policies for planning, recruitment, training, and retention of human resources for health (HRH), and improvement of access to the health-care workforce among populations. Using comparable and standardised data sources, we aim to describe the composition and density of health workers by sex among 20 cadres for 204 countries and territories over 1990-2023 and quantify workforce shortfalls relative to universal health coverage (UHC) attainment. METHODS: We used 1816 country-years of data from population-based surveys, 82 from censuses, 3888 from administrative sources, and 96 from scientific literature. We harmonised reported occupation in all sources with the International Standard Classification of Occupations 2008. We produced estimates for 20 cadres and the total health workforce disaggregated by sex using spatiotemporal Gaussian process regression, a standardised method in the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors study. Finally, stochastic frontier meta-regression was used to estimate the minimum density of doctors, nurses and midwives, dentists, and pharmacists required to reach a score of 80 out of 100 on the UHC effective coverage index. FINDINGS: In 2023, there were 122·1 million (95% uncertainty interval 115·4-130·5) health workers across 20 cadres, an increase of 81·2 million (72·0-90·5) or 198·5% (161·9-245·6) relative to 1990. Of that total, there were 15·1 million (13·1-18·2) doctors, 33·2 million (30·8-36·3) nurses, 2·4 million (2·0-2·9) midwives, and 7·6 million (6·7-8·6) community health workers (CHWs). 68·9% (66·9-70·6) of all health workers in 2023 were female, and female health workers accounted for 71·4% (64·5-77·4) of net HRH workforce growth. Less than half of doctors were female (43·9%, 34·5-53·2) and most nurses (80·7%, 76·2-83·1), midwives (96·0%, 83·9-98·5), and CHWs (89·5%, 83·6-93·7) were female. Substantial differences in HRH density remained into 2023: sub-Saharan Africa had the lowest HRH densities across cadres, with the exception of CHWs, while high-income countries had the highest HRH densities. To reach 80 out of 100 on the UHC index, an additional 7·1 million (6·6-7·5) doctors, 23·9 million (21·8-26·1) nurses and midwives, 1·8 million (1·6-1·9) dentists, and 1·6 million (1·4-1·9) pharmacists are required globally. INTERPRETATION: The global health workforce has expanded substantially since 1990, largely due to women entering the formal health workforce. However, this expansion has been uneven across regions and persistent shortfalls remain in doctors, nurses and midwives, dentists, and pharmacists relative to moderate UHC attainment. Addressing these gaps will require expansion of training capacity, retention and remuneration policies for early-career workers, and gender-responsive workforce arrangements. FUNDING: Gates Foundation.

title: Antenatal outcomes for women with multiple long-term conditions in pregnancy: a UK-wide retrospective cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Around 20% of pregnant women in the UK have multiple long-term conditions (MLTCs), defined as two or more physical or mental health conditions. The current evidence related to adverse maternal outcomes at a population level is scarce. The aim of this study was to compare antenatal outcomes between women with and without MLTCs across the four UK nations. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included pregnant women aged 15-49 years from England, Northern Ireland, Scotland, and Wales. Data sources included Clinical Practice Research Datalink Gold (CPRD; 2000-22), Born in Bradford (2006-10), Secure Anonymised Information Linkage (2000-19), Scottish routine health records (2010-19), and the Northern Ireland Maternity System (2011-21). MLTCs were defined using a list of 79 health conditions developed with input from women and clinicians, with the number of conditions recorded including the mental health conditions. Antenatal outcomes included miscarriage, venous thromboembolism, gestational hypertension, pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, obstetric cholestasis, vomiting and hyperemesis, and antenatal mental health outcomes (anxiety and depression). Modified Poisson regression was used to estimate the association between MLTCs and antenatal outcomes separately for each dataset, adjusting for maternal age, gravidity, ethnicity, deprivation, BMI, smoking, and year of pregnancy. Pooled estimates across datasets were derived through meta-analysis when outcomes were available. Miscarriage and termination of pregnancy were reported using CPRD only, whereas antenatal anxiety and depression were pooled across datasets when ascertainment was available. FINDINGS: A total of 2 225 701 pregnancies or birth events were analysed. Compared with women without MLTCs, those with MLTCs had increased risks of antenatal complications, including hyperemesis (adjusted risk ratio 1·69 [95% CI 1·58-1·81]), vomiting (1·61 [1·46-1·78]), miscarriage (1·20 [1·18-1·22]), gestational diabetes (1·26 [1·18-1·34]), gestational hypertension (1·18 [1·13-1·22]), obstetric cholestasis (1·28 [1·11-1·47]), pre-eclampsia (1·42 [1·25-1·61]), placental abruption (1·32 [1·22-1·44]), venous thromboembolism (2·19 [1·73-2·78]), antenatal anxiety (4·25 [2·59-6·99]), and depression (4·09 [3·27-5·11]). No significant associations were found for termination of pregnancy or chorioamnionitis. The risk of complications increased with the number of coexisting conditions. INTERPRETATION: Maternal MLTCs were associated with increased risk of antenatal complications. These findings highlight the urgent need for integrated care pathways and targeted risk assessment for pregnant women with MLTCs. FUNDING: Medical Research Council, National Institute for Health and Care Research, Economic and Social Research Council, Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.

title: Physical activity across work and leisure for dementia prevention
abstract: Randomised trials have shown that physical activity offers substantial health benefits (eg, preventing type 2 diabetes and falls and improving outcomes after myocardial infarction). Whether these benefits extend to dementia remains uncertain. Dementia has a preclinical phase that can last for decades, making prevention trials particularly challenging. Over such long periods, declining adherence in treatment groups and increasing physical activity in control participants reduce between-group differences and dilute treatment effects.

title: Beyond global counts: making health workforce estimates actionable and equitable
abstract: In The Lancet Public Health, the GBD 2023 Human Resources for Health Collaborators present an updated description of global health workforce numbers and distribution for the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023.1 The analysis of sex distribution is striking, with female health workers representing 69% of the health workforce and contributing to around three-quarters of its growth. The study also shows substantial differences across occupations, with 44% of medical doctors but 81% of nursing personnel being female, with wide country and regional differences.

title: Correction to Lancet Public Health 2026; 11: e506–17
Heat-health interventions for people experiencing homelessness
abstract: Extreme heat is intensifying globally and disproportionately harms people experiencing homelessness, who face continuous exposure and limited capacity to access cooling. We reviewed the literature on heat-protection interventions that report findings for people experiencing homelessness. Only 12 studies met the inclusion criteria, indicating a sparse and heterogeneous evidence base mainly from high-income countries (USA, Canada, and Australia). No eligible studies were identified from Europe despite substantial heat events in the region. Interventions included cooling centres and cooled public spaces (eg, air-conditioned community halls and libraries), outreach and preparedness programmes (eg, education and weather-preparedness kits), and makeshift shelter modifications (eg, tent shading and ventilation), with housing and temporary accommodation discussed as structural protection. Access barriers to cooled spaces were common (eg, transport constraints and rules restricting belongings or pets), and some participants relied on self-directed cooling strategies (eg, travelling on public transport) rather than services. Evaluations reported qualitative implementation outcomes and physiological and exposure outcomes, with limited clinical-outcome reporting, constraining inference about effects on heat-related morbidity or mortality. Future research should prioritise co-designed, hybrid models that combine accessible cooling centres and cooled public spaces with outreach and low-cost mobile or distributed cooling (eg, electric fans and water dousing), evaluated using standardised implementation metrics and broad health endpoints.

title: Global, regional, and national prevalence of second-hand smoke and attributable disease burden in 204 countries and territories, 1990–2023: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
authors: Sayed Muhammad Ata Ullah Shah Bukhari
abstract: BACKGROUND: Second-hand smoke (SHS) exposure remains a major source of morbidity and mortality among non-smokers. This study presents the first dedicated Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) publication to systematically quantify SHS prevalence and evaluate its effect as a global risk factor across a broader range of outcomes. METHODS: Using the GBD 2023 comparative risk assessment framework, we estimated SHS exposure prevalence and attributable disease burden across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023, stratified by age and sex. Exposure estimates were derived by synthesising population-based surveys and household composition data through spatiotemporal Gaussian process regression. Relative risks for nine health outcomes, now including asthma, were estimated using the Burden of Proof methodology, and applied to calculate attributable deaths and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs). FINDINGS: In 2023, an estimated 2·71 billion (95% UI 2·44-3·02) people worldwide were exposed to SHS, including 767 million (687-858) children aged 0-14 years. Age-standardised prevalence was highest in southeast Asia, east Asia, and Oceania (48·4% [44·0-53·4]), with female individuals in some countries experiencing nearly 1·8 times the exposure prevalence of male individuals. Despite a 22·2% (10·6-32·4) decline in global age-standardised prevalence since 1990, this progress has not been sufficient to reduce the absolute number of exposed individuals, which has remained stable globally and has risen sharply in sub-Saharan Africa (98·5% [62·0-144·4] increase) and North Africa and the Middle East (72·1% [47·8-101·8] increase). In 2023, SHS exposure accounted for 1·66 million (1·33-2·07) deaths and 44·8 million (35·8-54·3) DALYs globally. Ischaemic heart disease was the leading contributor to SHS-attributable DALYs (12·0 million [9·31-15·2]) overall, while lower respiratory infections predominated among children (5·16 million [3·48-7·12]). INTERPRETATION: We estimated that SHS remains a substantial driver of global health loss, particularly through cardiovascular and paediatric respiratory diseases. Persistent geographical disparities and growing absolute numbers of exposed individuals in several regions underscore the urgent need for accelerated implementation and enforcement of comprehensive tobacco control measures, particularly to protect women and children in both public and domestic environments. FUNDING: Bloomberg Philanthropies and the Gates Foundation.

title: Public health in a fracturing world: the erosion of the international rules-based order
abstract: One of the greatest threats to public health today is not any single disease, environmental hazard, or conflict, but the erosion of the international rules-based order that enables countries to cooperate in addressing shared risks. Over the past decade, public health has faced increasingly interconnected challenges, including climate change, conflict, pollution, emerging infectious diseases, food and water insecurity, mass displacement, and misinformation. These threats are amplified by fragile governance, growing inequality, and declining trust in institutions. Public health depends fundamentally on international cooperation. Surveillance systems, outbreak reporting, vaccine supply chains, environmental regulation, and climate adaptation all require shared rules, transparency, and trust between states. As these mechanisms weaken, risks become harder to manage and their effects more unequal. Public health should adapt by strengthening collaborative infrastructure, treating misinformation as a major health threat, investing in shared preparedness, and engaging more actively with trade, finance, climate, and security policies. Rebuilding effective international cooperation is essential to protecting health in an increasingly fragmented world.

title: The 2026 Europe Cities Report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change: cities at the forefront of climate change action
abstract: Translations For the French and Spanish translations of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

title: Effects of a healthy checkout ordinance on the sale of soft drinks and confectionery in Berkeley, CA, USA: a quasi-experimental study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Placing products in prominent locations such as store checkouts can promote impulse purchases of foods and beverages high in added sugars. On March 1, 2021, Berkeley, CA, USA, implemented the world's first mandatory healthy checkout ordinance (HCO), prohibiting the display of foods high in added sugars and sweetened beverages, including soft drinks (known as soda in the USA) and confectionery (known as candy in the USA), at store checkouts. The HCO was enforceable on Jan 1, 2022. We aimed to evaluate the association of the HCO with sales of soda (sweetened with sugar or non-sugar sweeteners) and candy in the city. METHODS: In this quasi-experimental study, we analysed Circana retail scanner data (March 3, 2019, to Dec 31, 2023) from 71 stores in Berkeley and three other comparison cities in California, restricted to chains operating in Berkeley. Data were point-of-sale records for selected food and beverage categories, which were aggregated by store and year-quarter for analysis. Primary outcomes were quarterly volume sales of soda and candy overall and by package size, using thresholds based on products commonly sold at checkouts. Using difference-in-differences regressions with store and year-quarter fixed effects, we estimated the association of the HCO with outcomes after its implementation and after it became enforceable. FINDINGS: Circana data included 71 (39%) of 183 identified standalone chain locations across the four cities: 19 (20%) of 93 supermarkets, 42 (59%) of 71 drugstores (ie, retail shops that combine a pharmacy with a general convenience store), and ten (53%) of 19 mass merchandisers. The analytical sample comprised more than 9 million product-store-month soda observations (1·0 million in Berkeley) and more than 52 million product-store-month candy observations (5·6 million in Berkeley), aggregated to 1420 store-quarter observations per outcome. After implementation, the estimated difference in mean soda sales was -2478 L per store-quarter (95% CI -5228 to 272; -23·4%), relative to comparison cities. After enforcement, soda sales were -3891 L per store-quarter (-7774 to -7; -39·5%). Estimates indicated reduced sales of large packages of soda after enforcement (-3800 L, -7571 to -30; -42·5%) and varied by store type. Overall candy sales increased after implementation (220 kg per store-quarter, 95% CI 21 to 420; 10·4%); after enforcement, the estimated difference was 156 kg (95% CI -78 to 390; 7·8%), with the 95% CI including the null. Supermarket sales of small packages of candy decreased by 132 kg after implementation (95% CI -212 to -51; -34·9%) and 156 kg after enforcement (-233 to -78; -43·2%). INTERPRETATION: Berkeley's mandatory HCO was found to be associated with decreased soda sales but not decreased overall candy sales after its enforcement. Estimates varied by product category, package size, and store type. Mandatory checkout standards can influence purchases, but implementation and enforcement strategies might need tailoring. FUNDING: US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases and Bloomberg Philanthropies.

title: Healthy checkout policies: a new front in food regulation
abstract: Prominent placement of junk food at store checkouts can prompt impulse purchasing, and checkout displays are encountered by nearly every shopper. Restrictions on the placement of less healthy products have rightly become a recognised part of the policy repertoire recommended to improve population diets, alongside taxation, marketing restrictions, and front-of-pack labelling. Evidence on their effects, however, comes largely from voluntary initiatives, single retail chains, or short observation periods.

title: Beyond individual-level approaches to dementia prevention: a socioecological reappraisal
abstract: Dementia prevention has largely focused on modifying individual behavioural and clinical risk factors. Although this approach has advanced understanding of dementia risk, it could under-recognise the broad social, environmental, and structural conditions that shape brain health across the life course. In this Viewpoint, we apply the socioecological model, a well established public health framework, to map 61 modifiable dementia risk and protective factors identified in the published population-attributable fraction literature across four levels of influence: individual, interpersonal, community, and societal. Most mapped factors (49/61 [80%]) were at the individual level, with few at interpersonal (2/61 [3%]), community (3/61 [5%]), or societal (7/61 [11%]) levels. This pattern suggests that the published evidence base remains predominantly organised around individual-level factors despite growing recognition of upstream influences. We argue that effective dementia prevention requires coordinated action across sectors, including education, urban planning, environmental policy, and health care.

title: Fit for the future: from siloed to integrated public health systems
abstract: Despite compelling evidence on the value of prevention, public health remains chronically underfunded and structurally deprioritised. Spending on prevention has remained stable at around 3% of total health expenditure across Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries for the past two decades, and despite a temporary doubling of spending during the COVID-19 pandemic, this trend has already reversed. The central challenge for the next decade lies not in the absence of evidence, but rather the absence of political will and systems capable of translating evidence into action. Three interconnected priorities stand out: (1) embedding public health in cross-sectoral governance frameworks so that prevention is assessed on equal terms with curative care; (2) strengthening data to support public health investment and budgeting, especially in a highly volatile fiscal environment for many countries; and (3) accelerating digital transformation to increase analytical ability, targeted public health intervention, and public trust. Progress in all three areas requires strong political leadership and rethinking current systems to ensure that they are fit for the future.

title: Causes of death across the life course in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN): a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
authors: Stephanie C C van der Lubbe
Mohammad Farris Iman Leong Bin Abdullah
abstract: BACKGROUND: The drivers of mortality and their associated risk factors evolve throughout the course of life. Understanding these transitions is essential for effective, equitable, and age-appropriate health interventions. METHODS: As part of the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) 2023, we examined life expectancy and the probability of death from birth to age 70 years (70q0) from 1990 to 2023 for each Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member state. In addition, we assessed causes of death and risk factor by age and sex across different life stages. Life expectancy was estimated from age-specific mortality rates with standard demographic techniques, and 70q0 from mortality and GBD life tables. Cause-specific mortality was estimated using the Cause of Death Ensemble model, and risk-attributable mortality using the comparative risk assessment framework. FINDINGS: In 2023, regional life expectancy was 70·1 years (95% uncertainty interval 69·6-70·7) for males and 76·2 years (75·7-76·7) for females, ranging from 87·5 years (87·3-87·8) for females in Singapore to 62·1 years (60·8-63·5) for males in Myanmar. Correspondingly, all-cause 70q0 was higher for males than for females. Neonatal disorders were the leading cause of mortality among infants younger than 1 year. Road injuries were the primary driver of mortality among males from adolescence through to early adulthood, accounting for 25·0% (17·0-31·0) of total mortality (8230 [5740-10 800] deaths) in males aged 15-19 years, with mortality rates varying from 3·0 per 100 000 population (2·3-3·7) to 49·0 per 100 000 population (25·0-67·1) between countries. Among females, maternal disorders were the leading cause of death in ages 25-34 years. In mid-adulthood, non-communicable diseases such as ischaemic heart disease and stroke emerged as major causes. Tobacco use was the dominant risk factor across most of adulthood in males, whereas high blood pressure was the prevailing risk factor among adult females. INTERPRETATION: Although the leading causes of death have converged across countries, the outcomes of these causes remain divergent, reflecting persistent inequalities across the region. These patterns present a strategic opportunity for multilateral action to mobilise collective resources and achieve regional health equity. FUNDING: Gates Foundation.

title: Childhood socioeconomic circumstances and adult mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Childhood socioeconomic circumstances are important determinants of adult health, yet no recent meta-analysis has quantified these associations or formally assessed evidence certainty. We aimed to synthesise evidence on associations between childhood socioeconomic circumstances and adult all-cause and cause-specific mortality. METHODS: For this systematic review and meta-analysis, we searched MEDLINE, SocIndex, ASSIA, and ProQuest Public Health from inception to May 26, 2026, without language restrictions, supplemented by backward citation searching. We included cohort studies examining associations between childhood socioeconomic conditions (parental education and occupation, economic circumstances, housing and material conditions, and composite indicators) and adult mortality (age ≥18 years), reporting quantitative estimates with extractable data. No randomised controlled trials were identified; all included studies were observational longitudinal studies. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-E and evidence certainty using GRADE. We pooled hazard ratios (HRs) using random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and calculated the relative index of inequality (RII) to enable standardised comparisons across exposure definitions. This study is registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024594671). FINDINGS: =90·1%; 18 studies), corresponding to 181 (95% CI 125-243) excess deaths per 100 000 population per year. Cause-specific analyses indicated elevated risks for cardiovascular (HR 1·26, 95% CI 1·13-1·42), respiratory (HR 1·70-1·85 across sex specific analyses), and lung cancer mortality (HR 1·52 in both sexes). The RII was highest for economic circumstances (RII 2·33, 95% CI 1·51-3·60) and parental education (RII 2·28, 1·60-3·26). Findings were consistent across exposure types, world regions, and risk of bias strata. 50 (49%) included studies were at high or very high risk of bias, primarily due to inadequate confounding control; sensitivity analyses restricted to lower risk of bias studies yielded consistent results. GRADE certainty ranged from very low to moderate. INTERPRETATION: Disadvantaged childhood socioeconomic circumstances are associated with increased adult mortality across diverse measures of disadvantage and causes of death, supporting prioritisation of early-life interventions to reduce long-term mortality inequalities. FUNDING: None.

title: From mortality patterns to regional action in ASEAN
The role of cities in public health
abstract: Has urban health become a singular public health success? In October, 2016, at the opening of the UN Habitat III conference on housing and sustainable urban development, former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said that cities were central to “global prosperity, peace and human rights,” and needed to be made “inclusive, safe, resilient, healthy and sustainable”. 10 years later, novel research in this issue of The Lancet Public Health shows that cities are now at the centre of public health both because of their agile governance structures and because of their susceptibility to health-harming urban environments.

title: Correction to Lancet Public Health 2022; 7: e763–74
Correction to Lancet Public Health 2026; 11: e797–818
Securing our global future: investing in adolescent health
abstract: Over the past decade, there has been growing recognition of adolescence as a unique developmental stage, across which focused interventions can reap a triple dividend of benefits: during adolescence itself, as adolescents mature into adulthood, and for the next generation parented by those adolescents. Yet, despite evidence of a ten-fold return on investment, adolescents remain largely invisible within the public health agenda and have not attracted the policy attention and financing needed for transformative change. Beyond prominent increases in obesity and mental ill health, immense challenges-climate disasters, conflict, pandemics, commercial interests, digital technologies, and political shifts-are reshaping young people's lives in ways that are more pervasive, complex, and severe than in the past. These threats risk reversing many of the gains in adolescent health over the past 20 years. Gender-sensitive and age-sensitive multisector interventions are needed to co-create opportunities that realise the potential of today's young people, which will help ensure the health and prosperity of future populations and the planet.

title: People at the centre
abstract: Since the 2024 US presidential election disruption of many US institutions, numerous leadership shifts and budget reallocations and reductions, along with legislative and policy changes, have shaken public health global financial architecture, damaging institutional global and domestic roles. Crucially, this fraught time also offers an opportunity to renavigate the positioning of the field of public health and the directions taken more than a century ago. In the 19th century the biomedical model became dominant and public health greatly reduced its focus on adverse living conditions-the previous strategy that underpinned many foundational advances as progressive elements of the sanitary movement allied with social movements to achieve better living conditions. Years later, this positioning left public health largely silent on growing corporate influence, privatisation, and inequality in income and wealth. The enduring US racial hierarchy also adds to the long odds of placing people at the centre-the overarching goal of improving people's health.

title: Outcomes of Mindful Mood Balance for Moms, online mindfulness-based cognitive therapy for perinatal depressive relapse prevention in the USA: a two-arm, single-blind, pragmatic randomised clinical trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Effective and accessible approaches to prevent depressive relapse and reduce symptoms are crucial for addressing the major public health problem of depression among perinatal women. We aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of Mindful Mood Balance (MMB) for Moms plus usual care (hereafter MMB for Moms)-a web-based mindfulness-based cognitive therapy programme customised for perinatal women-compared with usual care only, in reducing depressive relapse and symptoms. METHODS: This single-blind, randomised clinical trial was done across the USA, in euthymic pregnant women with recurrent depression who were on recent or current antidepressant medication. Recruitment occurred from March 7, 2019, to July 8, 2020 (data collection was completed Sept 12, 2021). Participants were randomly assigned to MMB for Moms, or usual care. Primary outcomes were reduction in depressive relapse risk and symptom burden, assessed using the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview and Patient Health Questionaire-9, respectively, across the study period. Outcomes were assessed from baseline until 6-months postpartum in three phases (intervention, end of intervention to delivery, and postpartum). The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03623620, and is complete. FINDINGS: Participants were recruited between March 7, 2019, and July 8, 2020. Data from 500 randomly assigned participants (mean age 32 years [SD 4·5] and mean 11·5 [2·8] weeks gestation), were analysed as the intention-to-treat sample. Of the 500 participants (249 assigned to MMB for Moms and 251 assigned to usual care), 383 [77%] provided assessment data at 3 months and 389 [78%] at 6 months postpartum. MMB for Moms had significantly lower risk of depressive relapse compared with usual care during the full trial period (up to 6 months postpartum): 81 (33%) of 249 participants assigned to MMB for Moms and 111 (44%) of 251 participants in usual care had depressive relapse (hazard ratio 0·74 [95% CI 0·56-0·99]; p=0·045; adjusted false discovery rate p=0·045). MMB for Moms was also associated with a significant reduction in depression symptom burden during the 12 week intervention phase (average decrease of 0·75 [SE 0·13] in the MMB for Moms group and 0·31 [0·13] in the usual care group) but not during the full trial period (average decrease of 0·61 [SE 0·18] in the MMB for Moms group and 0·54 [0·17] in the usual care group). INTERPRETATION: MMB for Moms resulted in lower risk of relapse compared with usual care, and lower depression symptom burden during the intervention phase, potentially offering an effective non-pharmacological support option for depression relapse prevention during the perinatal period with positive implications for public health practice. FUNDING: US National Institutes of Health and US National Institute of Mental Health.

title: Association between parental death during childhood and health and wellbeing in adulthood in 22 countries and regions: a retrospective, outcome-wide analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Clinical and epidemiological evidence suggests that adults who have experienced the death of a parent or caregiver in childhood are at elevated risk for adverse health outcomes. The aim of this study was to examine cross-national variation in indicators of health and wellbeing among adults who experienced the death of a parent by age 12 years. METHODS: In this retrospective, outcome-wide analysis, we analysed data from Wave 1 of the Global Flourishing Study, a 5-year pre-registered longitudinal panel study (2024-28) of nationally representative adult participants (N=202 898) aged 18 years and older using probability-sampling across 22 geographically and culturally diverse countries and regions (ie, Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Egypt, Germany, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Israel, Japan, Kenya, Mexico, Nigeria, the Philippines, Poland, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Tanzania, Türkiye, the UK, and the USA) to examine associations between retrospectively recalled parental death during childhood (yes or no) and current health and wellbeing. We conducted a series of country and region-specific weighted multivariable regression using an outcome-wide design. Random effects meta-analyses were used to pool country and region-specific effect estimates for 69 wellbeing outcomes. FINDINGS: Meta-analysed associations across 22 countries and regions suggested that participants who experienced the death of a parent by age 12 years, relative to those who did not, reported more age-normalised health impairments (risk ratio [RR] 1·14 [95% CI 1·04 to 1·25]), more anxiety and depression symptoms (RR 1·09 [1·01 to 1·17] and RR 1·08 [1·01 to 1·15], respectively), more loneliness (standardised effect estimate [B] 0·06 [95% CI 0·01 to 0·10]), reduced sense of meaning (B -0·05 [-0·08 to -0·01], and reduced wellbeing (for example a lower sense of being at peace [RR 0·96 (95% CI 0·92 to 0·99)]). Country-specific effect estimates varied in magnitude. INTERPRETATION: Parental bereavement in childhood can affect health and wellbeing in adulthood, with some cross-national variation in the magnitude of adverse effects. Parental death during childhood is an important determinant of health across the lifespan and as such public health policies are needed to support a population-wide approach to bereavement care that spans health, social, and economic domains. FUNDING: John Templeton Foundation, Templeton Religion Trust, Templeton World Charity Foundation, Fetzer Institute, Paul Foster Family Foundation, Wellbeing for Planet Earth Foundation, Well Being Trust, and the David and Carol Myers Foundation.

title: The epistemic crisis as the defining challenge of public health: knowledge, power, and the politics of truth
abstract: Public health has always been a science in the service of politics-a discipline that translates evidence into collective action and knowledge into policy. But something qualitatively different is now under way. The next decade will not merely test the capacity of public health to respond to new threats, it will test the epistemic foundations on which the entire enterprise rests. The crisis we face is not primarily a crisis of evidence-there is more health research than ever-but of the authority of knowledge: who produces it, whose counts, and whether shared facts can still ground collective responses.

title: Are there grounds for optimism for the future of global health?
abstract: In the past decade, the field of global health has faced severe challenges and intense scrutiny concerning its legitimacy and effectiveness. A longer-term perspective-200 years rather than 10-offers grounds for guarded optimism about the future of global health. A review of the history of international health reveals that although the self-interested agendas of industrialised states have been the dominant driving forces in the field, these pursuits have been tempered by the gradual cross-national diffusion of cosmopolitan norms and initiatives concerning the right to health for all and government responsibility to improve population health. The grounds for hope are not that progress is inevitable. Rather, universalist commitments might have become sufficiently widespread and institutionalised to withstand periods of political backlash without reversing long-term expansion. The key to sustaining progress will be that actors who are committed to these norms persist in defending them.

title: Reimagining the aspirations of public health for the coming decade
abstract: The past 10 years have challenged and reshaped public health in ways that were difficult to imagine more than a decade ago. This situation calls on public health to think clearly about where the field is headed and to anticipate where the field needs to be so as to emerge stronger from the moment. Five trends will be shaping health in the coming decades: population ageing, urbanisation, climate change, changing relationships with institutions, and the emergence of transformative technology. These trends are driving-and coinciding with-shifting disease burden, including the rise of non-communicable diseases, the growing importance of neurological diseases and brain disorders, the continued and more unpredictable effects of infectious diseases, widening health gaps, and increasing demands on health systems. These challenges present clear opportunities and should focus public health on five key aspirations moving forward: creating longer, healthier lives through a reckoning with the conditions for healthy ageing, grappling with new-and primarily commercial-determinants of health, efforts to build better health systems, the embrace of new technologies, and a reimagination of how the field thinks, talks, acts, and communicates its work.

title: The north–south divide in English mortality, 1981–2024: a longitudinal population study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The north-south mortality divide in England, UK, has persisted for several decades. Previous longitudinal analyses up to 2016 have highlighted a widening mortality gap among those aged 25-44 years since the mid-1990s. We aimed to update mortality trends in England and evaluate how trends differed by age and sex up to 2024. METHODS: We did a segmented longitudinal population study of the north-south mortality divide in England (1981-2024). Using registered deaths and mid-year population estimates by 5-year age group and sex, we calculated standardised mortality rates and estimated adjusted north-south rate ratios using within-year Poisson models. We used segmented Poisson regression to compare mortality trends between 2010-19 and 2020-24. FINDINGS: Despite overall declines in mortality, interrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, the north-south mortality divide persisted during 1981-2024, widening among both female and male individuals aged 25-49 years. During 2010-19, northern excess mortality among those aged 25-49 years increased per year for female individuals (incidence rate ratio 1·018 [95% CI 1·013-1·022]) and male individuals (1·012 [1·009-1·016]). During 2020-24, these trends continued: Poisson models suggested a slowing among female individuals aged 25-49 years (0·987 [0·975-0·999]) and further widening among male individuals younger than 75 years (1·004 [1·000-1·007]), but neither change was robust to allowance for overdispersion, and the gap did not narrow in any age or sex group. By 2024, northern excess mortality reached 25·9% (95% CI 24·7-27·1) for those younger than 75 years, and 42·4% (38·5-46·3) for those aged 25-49 years. INTERPRETATION: Over the past four decades, England's regional mortality inequalities have widened among working‑age adults, with more rapid increases among female individuals than male individuals up to 2020 (before the COVID-19 pandemic). Pre-pandemic trends continued through 2020-24, with no narrowing of the north-south gap in any age or sex group by 2024. Reducing the north-south health divide will require sustained large-scale action across central government and regional authorities. FUNDING: National Institute for Health and Care Research, British Heart Foundation, and The Pandemic Institute.

title: The effect of food taxes in the UK on health and economic outcomes, and equity: a modelling study
abstract: BACKGROUND: WHO recommends using fiscal policies (such as taxes on unhealthy foods) that discourage consuming foods that contribute to unhealthy diets. Food tax evaluations require consideration for sociodemographic differences, consumer and industry behaviour, reformulation, and long-term health-related outcomes and health inequalities. We aimed to model the potential benefits and harms of three food tax policy designs, to health, costs, and inequalities, in the UK. METHODS: Using a microsimulation model, we performed an economic evaluation of three UK food tax policy designs: (1) a Sugar Snacks tax targeting snacks, cakes, and milk drinks; (2) an Unhealthy Food tax high in fat, sugar, or salt; and (3) a Sugar and Salt tax. Consumption and nutritional changes for a UK representative synthetic population (aged ≥5 years) were estimated by applying a hierarchical Almost Ideal Demand System, accommodating key socio-demographic differences. Our primary analysis simulated outcomes for consumer response only. Secondary analyses incorporated industry responses in the model. The microsimulation estimated changes to weight, cardiometabolic risk factors, lifetime health, discounted National Health Service (NHS) costs, social care costs, unemployment or inactivity, and social benefit receipts. FINDINGS: The estimated average reduction in daily calorie intake was -25 kcal (95% credible interval [95% CrI]; -31 to -19), -42 kcal (-51 to -33), and -58 kcal (-66 to -50) for the Sugar Snacks, Unhealthy Food, and Sugar and Salt taxes respectively, with reductions in sugar, salt, and saturated fat. Long-term modelling showed improved health, including reduced cardiovascular disease, and type 2 diabetes for all three tax policies. The taxes reduced NHS costs (Sugar Snacks -£168 [95% CrI -461 to -73], Unhealthy Food -£268 [-722 to -105], and Sugar and Salt -£374 [-1033 to -159]) and social care costs. The impact on health inequalities varied by policy design. Only the Sugar and Salt tax had a positive impact on health inequalities. INTERPRETATION: The overall health impact of each of the three tax policy designs modelled was positive, but it can be associated with important nutritional trade-off-cross-price elasticities led to a reduction in fibre intake. Of the three policies modelled, the Sugar and Salt tax generated the greatest gains and reduced health inequalities. Policy design should consider potential impacts on health inequalities and should be part of a multi-component strategy. FUNDING: National Institute for Health and Care Research.

title: Closing the implementation gap: prioritised, proactive, and accountable primary health care for the next decade
abstract: Most preventable deaths in low-income and middle-income countries occur not because effective interventions are unknown or unaffordable but because health systems fail to deliver these interventions reliably. Primary health care is essential for public health: prevention, early detection, and treatment can reach entire populations. Nearly 50 years after the Alma-Ata Declaration, few primary health-care systems effectively prevent, detect, and treat the leading killers. Two forces make now the moment to act: the abrupt 2025 decrease in development assistance and new technologies that might improve the ability to deliver and measure care at low cost. To close this implementation gap, primary health care should be prioritised, proactive, and accountable. Prioritised primary health care within a commitment to universal primary health care should fund the highest-impact actions first with transparent, nationally owned selection, and with core essential medicines free at the point of dispensing. Proactive primary health care should reach, track, and support patients before and between visits. Accountable primary health care should judge success by health outcomes with financing aligned with population health goals. Preventable deaths should be reviewed without blame as never-events feeding into improved prioritisation. Delivering these actions requires a skilled and supported workforce, a reliable supply of medicines and diagnostics, sustained financing, community trust, and data that can drive action. Decide first which outcomes matter most, identify the actions that produce them, strengthen the system those actions require, and judge investment by health gained.

title: A multifaceted intervention to increase bystander CPR rates after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in France: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised, controlled trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is a key determinant of survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but rates remain suboptimal worldwide. We evaluated whether a multifaceted intervention targeting emergency dispatch systems and community response could increase bystander-initiated CPR before emergency medical service (EMS) arrival. METHODS: We conducted a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial in 15 French EMS agencies. The intervention combined dispatcher training for early recognition of cardiac arrest and telephone-assisted CPR, activation of trained volunteers through a geolocation smartphone application, and structured audit and feedback provided to EMS agencies. Consecutive adults (≥18 years) with non-traumatic OHCA were included. Randomisation was stratified by tercile of OHCA volume managed by each EMS in 2015. The intervention was implemented during a 1-month transition period before the intervention period at each EMS centre. A dedicated protocol guided dispatchers to identify cardiac arrest from unresponsiveness and abnormal breathing, then gave scripted compression-only instructions and activated volunteers, targeting recognition within 60 s of call pick-up and first compression within a further 60 s. The primary outcome was bystander-initiated CPR before EMS arrival. The trial was prospectively registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03633370) and is completed. FINDINGS: Of the 15 EMS agencies initially randomised, two withdrew before recruitment began and were replaced, and one enrolled no patients. Therefore, between Aug 27, 2018, and Feb 20, 2022, 14 EMS agencies recruited a total of 2160 patients. The intention-to-treat analysis included 1684 patients (686 control, 998 intervention) enrolled across the 12 originally randomised EMS agencies. The mean age for all patients included in the intention-to-treat analysis was 67 years (SD 15), and 1205 (71·6%) were male. Bystander-initiated CPR before EMS arrival occurred in 421 (61·4%) patients in the control group and 708 (70·9%) patients in the intervention group (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1·54 [95% CI 1·09-2·19]; p=0·017). Estimates were consistent across six prespecified sensitivity analyses (OR range, 1·38-1·55), remaining significant in four, but not after adjustment for cluster-specific secular trends (1·38 [0·98-1·94]) or baseline characteristics (1·39 [0·97-1·98]). No intervention-related adverse events were reported. INTERPRETATION: A multifaceted intervention was associated with increased bystander-initiated CPR after OHCA, although the estimate was sensitive to the modelling of secular trends, and it did not translate into improved clinical outcomes. These findings support further investigation of coordinated community-based strategies to strengthen the early links in the chain of survival at a population level. FUNDING: Direction Générale de l'Offre de Soins.

title: Investing in pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response
abstract: If resources for public health and decision makers are limited, what are the highest-priority investments they can make? Drawing on the Disease Control Priorities report on pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response, in this Viewpoint we summarise our reflections and recommendations for the next decade in public health and focus on the highest return actions for pandemic preparedness, prevention, and response that countries can take to protect themselves and others. We identified 85 feasible national-level and local-level actions, categorising 40 of them as high-priority investments. At regional and global levels, we identified and recommend 33 high-priority actions. These investments could have pay-offs substantially exceeding their cost. Ensuring adequate funding will require countries to contribute according to their fiscal capacity, with some countries requiring external support. Importantly, financing response to an outbreak should be timely and therefore prearranged.

title: Prison health-care governance and public health: a call for research
abstract: Despite the disproportionate burden of health disorders in people who are imprisoned, and the public health implications of these health disorders, responsibility for prison health care has historically rested with justice authorities rather than with the national health systems.

title: The urgent role for health professionals in accelerating mitigation and adaptation to climate change
abstract: Populations worldwide face unprecedented dangers from rapid climate change. The past 11 years have been the hottest on record.1 The 2025 Lancet Countdown report documented record-breaking health impacts and risks across 65% of the climate change health threats it monitors. Many records continue to be broken annually: 2026 had the hottest July on record; east Asia and much of Europe had unprecedented heatwaves with record heat-related deaths; and Germany alone registered 14 000 deaths by early August.

title: Public health has a mobilisation problem
abstract: The past decade has transformed public health. We can measure health loss with unprecedented precision, identify its causes and risks, and expose inequalities between and within populations. The Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) exemplifies this progress:1 its latest cycle estimates the burden of 375 diseases and injuries and 88 modifiable risks across 204 countries and territories.2

title: Addressing health equity and its major challenges
abstract: Three major challenges confront public health: inequality, the climate crisis, and political instability. Four domains of recommendations, formulated to respond to the inequality-pandemic cycle, form the basis of what is needed to improve health and health equity. First, address the gross inequalities in the global, and national, economic architecture. Second, take action on the social determinants of health-the eight Marmot Principles provide an evidence-based guide to action. Third, ensure an equitable distribution of health-enhancing technology. Finally, enable community development. Marmot Places, which have been developed in England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland, are a way to combine domains two and four: taking action on social determinants of health at the local level. However, national action is required too, particularly on unfair economic arrangements.

title: Preventing perinatal depression relapse
abstract: Mental health conditions are a leading cause of pregnancy-related deaths in the USA, affecting at least 20% of individuals in pregnancy and postpartum.1 Psychiatric relapse and emergencies in the perinatal period are disproportionately greater for women with a history of depression than for those without.2 Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy leverages cognitive behavioural therapy and meditative mindfulness practice to improve depression symptoms and prevent relapse among perinatal individuals with recurrent depression.

title: To increase bystander CPR rates after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, bystanders alone are not sufficient
abstract: Despite decades-long efforts by emergency medical services (EMS) to improve clinical outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), efficient strategies are still lacking. With a global incidence as high as around 50 per 100 000 person-years, a critically unfavourable relationship between no-flow duration (the time elapsed from collapse to the first cardiopulmonary resuscitation [CPR] measures) and survival, EMS response times that cannot be made faster, low survival rates, and poor neurological status among survivors despite advanced life support,1 OHCA still represents a substantial health-care challenge.

title: The Lancet Public Health at 10
abstract: This issue of The Lancet Public Health marks the journal's 10th anniversary. In 2016, after witnessing two Public Health Emergencies of International Concern—epidemics of Zika and Ebola virus—The Lancet team decided to launch an open access journal in public health, underlining the importance of the free availability of research findings for public health practice and policy decision making. Over the past decade, we have sought to address the most urgent issues in public health, to document and respond to new and emerging predicaments (eg, the environmental and commercial determinants of health), and to shed light on some under-recognised, underestimated determinants of health and health equity.

title: A more complete global picture of acute poisoning is required
abstract: In The Lancet Public Health, the GBD 2023 Poisoning Collaborators published updated estimates for the number of deaths that occurred in 2023 from unintentional acute poisoning worldwide.1 They report 2·54 million poisoning cases, resulting in 69 805 deaths, and a loss of 3·68 million age-standardised disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs). Carbon monoxide poisoning accounted for 44·3% of deaths while poisoning by other means (predominantly due to pesticide poisoning) accounted for 55·7%. Good news comes from an overall 47·5% reduction in DALY loss since 1990.

title: Global, regional, and national burden of unintentional poisoning, 1990–2023: results from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
authors: Syed Zeeshan Haider Zeeshan Haider Naqvi
abstract: BACKGROUND: Unintentional poisoning is a preventable cause of injury-related morbidity and mortality, yet global patterns, trends, and inequalities remain incompletely characterised. Within the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) framework, unintentional poisoning includes poisoning by carbon monoxide and poisoning by other means, a category largely informed by pesticide poisoning codes plus some indirect capture of other poisoning as part of the GBD re-distribution process. Poisonings by pharmaceuticals and illicit substances are not captured in the GBD definition of poisoning. We aimed to quantify this GBD-defined burden and assess regional variation, sociodemographic gradients, and case fatality between 1990 and 2023. METHODS: We analysed GBD 2023 estimates for 204 countries and territories, modelling deaths, incidence, and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) using standard GBD cause-of-death and non-fatal estimation methods with 95% uncertainty intervals. We stratified results by age, sex, region, and Socio-demographic Index (SDI), and derived case fatality from modelled deaths and incidence. FINDINGS: In 2023, unintentional poisoning from carbon monoxide and other means caused 2·54 million incident poisonings, 69 805 deaths, and 3·68 million DALYs globally, with age-standardised DALY rates declining by 47·5% since 1990. Carbon monoxide accounted for 641 932 poisonings, 30 890 deaths and 1·34 million DALYs, with the highest burdens in central and eastern Europe and central Asia. Most regions showed substantial long-term declines, and the global age-standardised DALY rate for carbon monoxide poisoning declined by 58·2% since 1990. Poisoning by other means caused 1·90 million incident cases, 38 914 deaths, and 2·34 million DALYs, with the greatest burden in sub-Saharan Africa. Most regions showed declining age-standardised DALY rates for poisoning by other means; however, there was no clear change (with the 95% uncertainty interval including zero) in the global estimate, driven by wide uncertainty intervals in several regions (including sub-Saharan Africa). Mortality and DALYs were inversely associated with SDI, and derived case fatality was highest in low-SDI regions. INTERPRETATION: Global reductions in GBD-defined unintentional poisoning by carbon monoxide and other means are consistent with decades of regulatory and environmental interventions. These include bans of highly toxic pesticides, improved heating and ventilation systems, emissions controls, and adoption of carbon monoxide alarms. Stark inequalities persist in some regions and in low-SDI settings. Compared with previous GBD publications, this study provides a detailed global assessment of unintentional poisoning by carbon monoxide and other means up to 2023, integrating incidence, DALYs, and comparative case fatality across regions. FUNDING: Gates Foundation and the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council.

title: The 2026 China report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change: safeguarding individual health through accelerated climate action
abstract: China experienced a distinctly warm and wet year in 2025, the highest number of hot days on record and the second-highest frequency of protracted extreme heat events. Record-breaking rainfall and rain-season duration was observed in north China, and the wettest autumn rainfall on record was seen in west China. These climate conditions pose increasing and uneven climate-related health risks to the Chinese population.

title: Skin health in China
abstract: The landscape of dermatological disease in China reflects the global skin health transition—ie, the shift in the major causes of skin disease burden from infectious diseases to non-communicable diseases. With its rapid pace of change (eg, urbanisation, industrialisation, and population ageing) and large population, China offers an example of how socioeconomic development might shape skin health. Skin health, in turn, provides insight into systemic health through its links with metabolism and immunity.

title: Trends, ethnic inequalities, and determinants of multiple nutrition-related health outcomes among Chinese children and adolescents aged 7–18 years: evidence from four national school health surveys, 2005–19
abstract: BACKGROUND: Eliminating all forms of malnutrition is essential for optimal child and adolescent development. In multi-ethnic China, nutrition-related conditions coexist, but ethnic-group patterns remain unclear. We assessed trends, between-ethnic inequalities, and co-occurrence among the Han majority and 26 ethnic minority groups. METHODS: We analysed four cross-sectional national school health surveys from 2005 to 2019, including 1 201 557 students aged 7-18 years. We estimated age-standardised and sex-standardised prevalence, ethnicity-level sociodemographic index (SDI) inequalities, and co-occurrence; anaemia analyses included 389 124 participants aged 7, 9, 12, and 14 years. Contextual associations and model-based population-attributable fractions (PAFs) were examined. FINDINGS: Between 2005 and 2019, overweight and obesity increased from 9·77% (95% CI 9·67-9·88) to 20·06% (19·92-20·20), obesity from 3·27% (3·21-3·34) to 8·18% (8·08-8·28), and high blood pressure from 8·81% (8·71-8·90) to 13·39% (13·28-13·51); stunting declined from 5·16% (5·08-5·24) to 2·12% (2·07-2·17) and thinness from 4·86% (4·78-4·94) to 2·55% (2·50-2·61), whereas anaemia remained prevalent (9·42% [9·24-9·60] in 2005 vs 10·40% [10·20-10·59] in 2019). Stunting remained concentrated among lower-SDI ethnic groups, whereas obesity and overweight and obesity were concentrated among higher-SDI groups and absolute inequalities widened. Among children with anaemia, overweight and obesity increased from 7·89% (7·32-8·46) to 18·19% (17·37-19·01); among those with stunting, overweight and obesity increased from 2·44% (2·18-2·70) to 6·89% (6·15-7·62). Higher education, health, and urbanisation indicators were associated with lower stunting odds; model-based joint PAFs were 16·39% for obesity and 22·01% for high blood pressure. INTERPRETATION: Across multi-ethnic China, the nutrition transition remains incomplete, with anaemia remaining common, stunting declining but persisting in some ethnic groups, and overweight and obesity and high blood pressure rising. Ethnic heterogeneity and increasing within-person co-occurrence of nutrition-related outcomes reveal an increasingly complex burden and limits of single-condition approaches, calling for integrated surveillance and tailored responses. FUNDING: National Key R&D Program of China, National Natural Science Foundation of China, Beijing Natural Science Foundation, Peking University Talent Introduction Program Project, and Peking University Health Science Center Innovation Fund for Outstanding Doctoral Students.

title: Prevalence and spectrum of skin diseases in adults in China: a nationwide cross-sectional study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Skin diseases have been identified as a public health priority at the 78th World Health Assembly, with a call for strengthened national surveillance and evidence-based responses. However, in China, comprehensive national epidemiological data on the prevalence of skin diseases have been lacking. We aimed to bridge this data gap by conducting the China Skin Health study, a large-scale, population-based, cross-sectional study. METHODS: In this study, we used a multistage stratified cluster random sampling design to obtain a nationally representative sample of adults aged 18 years or older from diverse geographical regions of China. We collaborated with provincial centres for disease control and prevention to establish a survey team comprising public health workers and ten to 12 certified dermatologists in each of the five provinces selected for the study. Residents' committees disseminated study information through posters and WeChat groups to recruit participants, and data were collected at local community health centres. Standardised electronic questionnaires were administered by trained interviewers to collect information on demographic and other characteristics. Certified dermatologists examined sun-exposed areas (eg, scalp, face, neck, and extremities) in all participants, as well as unexposed areas reported as concerns by respondents, for common skin diseases spanning 12 categories and more than 60 specific conditions. Clinical diagnoses were made on the basis of observed skin manifestations.
